title: HTTP Headers Deep Dive: Negotiation, Ranges, Compression & Security
summary: A dense-notes carousel covering how HTTP headers drive content negotiation, range downloads, compression, browser security (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options), and custom header conventions — with mechanics, gotchas, and practical recipes.

chapters.title: Headers 101: Structure & Categories
points: Header = case-insensitive 'Name: value' pairs; multiple values comma-separated or repeated lines
Four categories: general, request, response, entity (representation) headers
End-to-end vs hop-by-hop headers (Connection, Keep-Alive are hop-by-hop)
Syntax rules per RFC 9110: no leading/trailing whitespace in field values, obs-fold deprecated
Field ordering doesn't matter semantically — except Set-Cookie quirks via proxies
Response header examples: Server, Date, Content-Length, Content-Type
Request header examples: Host (mandatory in HTTP/1.1), User-Agent, Referer (misspelled on purpose)
HTTP/2 & 3 lowercase headers + HPACK/QPACK compression; 'Host' becomes ':authority'
Size budgets: browsers/proxies often cap headers ~8–16 KB per side
Inspect with curl -v, browser DevTools Network tab, or httpie -v
Gotcha: duplicate headers with conflicting meaning → undefined behavior; join with commas
Trade-off: every header costs bytes on the wire — trim unnecessary ones on CDNs

chapters.title: Content Negotiation: Accept & Friends
points: Proactive (server-driven) negotiation: client states preferences, server picks representation
Four dimensions: Accept (media type), Accept-Language, Accept-Charset (deprecated), Accept-Encoding
Media range syntax: type/subtype, type/*, */*; quality values q=0..1, default q=1
Specificity beats q: text/html beats text/* beats */* regardless of q
Example: Accept: text/html;q=0.9, application/json;q=0.8, */*;q=0.1
Server returns 406 Not Acceptable only when nothing acceptable AND no fallback chosen
Vary: response header lists request headers that affect the representation — required for caching
Reactive (agent-driven) negotiation: server offers choices via 300 Multiple Choices / Allow
API design: negotiate via Accept header vs URL extension (.json) vs query param (?format=json)
Accept* headers drive CDN/proxy cache keys — missing Vary = serving wrong language/type
Gotcha: browsers send Accept: */* on fetch/XHR by default — you often negotiate manually
Testing: curl -H 'Accept: application/xml' https://api.example.com/data

chapters.title: Range Requests: Resumable & Partial Content
points: Client requests partial bytes: Range: bytes=0-499 (first 500) or bytes=500- (open-ended)
Server support signal: Accept-Ranges: bytes in a normal 200 response
Success response: 206 Partial Content + Content-Range: bytes 0-499/12345
Unsatisfiable range → 416 Range Not Satisfiable with Content-Range: bytes */12345
Suffix ranges bytes=-500 = last 500 bytes; overlapping multiple ranges in one request
Multiple ranges → multipart/byteranges response, one part per range with its own headers
Resume a failed download: If-Range with ETag or Last-Modified to avoid stale-part mixing
If the resource changed since the 206 started, If-Range fails → server sends fresh 200
Use cases: video seeking, download managers, PDF page loading, resumable uploads (tus-style)
Gotcha: 206 must NOT be cached as if it were the full representation; Vary/ETag must match
Servers/CDNs may ignore Range (send 200) — clients must handle both
Validate: curl -H 'Range: bytes=0-99' -i url → expect 206 and 100 bytes

chapters.title: Accept-Encoding & Content Compression
points: Client offers codecs: Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd; identity = no compression
Server confirms actual codec via Content-Encoding: gzip (never send unoffered encoding)
Order = preference: br, gzip; modern browsers add zstd (Chrome 117+)
Brotli vs gzip: ~15–20% smaller, but slower to compress — great for static pre-compression
zstd: near-brotli ratio, much faster compression/decompression — rising default for dynamic
Static assets: pre-compress at build time (file.br, file.gz) — best ratio, zero CPU at request time
Dynamic responses: compress on the fly with level ~4–6 gzip; watch CPU on high traffic
Content-Length reflects compressed size; chunked transfer if length unknown
Never compress already-compressed media (JPEG, video, ZIP) — wastes CPU, can grow size
BREACH/CRIME: compressing responses with secrets + attacker-reflected input can leak data
Mitigate BREACH: random padding, CSRF token rotation, or disable compression on sensitive routes
Vary: Accept-Encoding is mandatory or proxies serve gzipped to clients that can't decode
Debug: check Network → Response Headers; verify Size (transfer) vs actual content size

chapters.title: Security Headers: The First Line of Defense
points: Security headers are response headers instructing the browser's security policy
CSP restricts what the page may load/execute; HSTS forces HTTPS; XFO/X-Frame-Options blocks framing
Also in the family: Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Headers only work as response headers — sending them in requests does nothing
Deploy at CDN/reverse-proxy level for consistency, not app-by-app
Test with securityheaders.com grade scan and browser console CSP violation reports
Missing headers = XSS, clickjacking, mixed-content, and MIME-sniffing attack surface
They complement (never replace) server-side auth checks and output escaping
Add headers early in the request lifecycle so error pages get them too
Report-Only variants (CSP, Permissions-Policy reporting) let you test without breaking
Oversized headers waste bytes: keep CSP concise, use hashes/nonces not huge whitelists
Remember: headers are advisory to the browser — non-browser clients ignore them entirely

chapters.title: Content-Security-Policy in Depth
points: Directive model: default-src, script-src, style-src, img-src, connect-src, frame-ancestors, etc.
Fallback chain: unspecified directives fall back to default-src; frame-ancestors ignores it
Sources: 'self', host patterns, https:, 'none', 'unsafe-inline', 'unsafe-eval'
Nonce-based scripts: script-src 'nonce-r4nd0m' — rotate per response, unguessable
Hash-based scripts: script-src 'sha256-...' for static inline blocks
Strict-Dynamic: nonce-approved script may load further scripts — modern recommended baseline
Danger: 'unsafe-inline' + 'unsafe-eval' largely defeats XSS protection
object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self' — three cheap hard wins
Reporting: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only + report-uri/report-to for safe rollout
Gotcha: CSP does NOT protect against server-side vulns or trusted-domain compromise (JSONP on allowed host)
Gotcha: inline event handlers (onclick) and style attributes blocked unless allowed explicitly
Example: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-X'; object-src 'none'

chapters.title: HSTS, X-Frame-Options & Frame Control
points: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload
Mechanics: browser caches the policy on first HTTPS response; future http:// URLs auto-upgrade to https://
First-visit gap: HSTS can't protect the very first request — hence the preload list
Gotcha: HSTS is sticky — misconfigured max-age or subdomains can lock sites out until max-age expires
Roll out gradually: short max-age first (e.g., 300), then raise; submit to hstspreload.org carefully
X-Frame-Options: DENY | SAMEORIGIN — legacy clickjacking defense
XFO is superseded by CSP frame-ancestors (supports origins, XFO does not)
Best practice: send BOTH XFO and frame-ancestors for old browsers
Clickjacking attack recap: invisible iframe + overlaid UI triggers user actions
ALLOW-FROM is dead — unsupported by modern browsers, don't ship it
Cross-origin embed use case: use frame-ancestors with the partner origin list instead
Bonus hardening: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff + correct Content-Type prevents MIME confusion

chapters.title: Caching & Conditional Headers Interplay
points: ETag / Last-Modified: validators returned with a representation
Conditional requests: If-None-Match → 304 Not Modified; If-Modified-Since for date validators
Strong vs weak ETags: W/"..." allows semantically-equal matches; strong = byte-identical
Cache-Control directives: max-age, no-cache (revalidate), no-store (never persist), private/public
must-revalidate / stale-while-revalidate / stale-if-error control freshness fallbacks
Vary ties everything together: cache key = URL + listed request headers (Accept, Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language)
Range + caching: full 200 response may satisfy a range request; intermediaries must coalesce carefully
ETag consistency requirement: same ETag across all nodes of a load-balanced cluster, or spurious 200s
Immutable + max-age=31536000 for fingerprinted assets (app.9f3c2.js) — the standard strategy
Gotcha: no-cache ≠ no-store; no-cache means 'store but revalidate'
304 saves body bytes but not the request — pair with long max-age to eliminate requests
Debug: DevTools shows '(from disk cache)', '304 Not Modified', or full 200 per resource

chapters.title: Custom Header Conventions
points: Naming: X-Prefix is deprecated by RFC 6648 — new headers just use descriptive names
Keep custom app headers namespaced: Api-Version, RateLimit-Remaining, Request-Id
Vendor trees still legit: x-amz-*, x-goog-* — namespaced by organization, not just 'X-'
Follow existing ecosystem conventions: Link, Retry-After, Location, Warning instead of inventing
Rate limiting convention: RateLimit-Limit / RateLimit-Remaining / RateLimit-Reset (draft RFC)
Request tracing: X-Request-Id / traceparent (W3C Trace Context) for distributed tracing
Documentation: every custom header needs docs — name, type, allowed values, default, mutability
Case-insensitivity reminder: clients may send api-version; canonicalize when reading
Size discipline: don't stuff payloads into headers; move data to body for anything large
Security: never trust client-sent identity headers (X-Forwarded-For, X-User-Id) without proxy sanitization
X-Forwarded-* family: For, Proto, Host — set only by trusted reverse proxies; strip from external input
Versioning & deprecation: Deprecation + Sunset headers to announce API retirement

chapters.title: Summary: Debugging Checklist & Mental Model
points: Mental model: request headers = client's offer/preferences; response headers = server's decision & policy
Negotiation trio: Accept* (request) → Content-* (response) → Vary (cache binding)
Range flow: Accept-Ranges → Range → 206 + Content-Range; resume via If-Range
Compression flow: Accept-Encoding → Content-Encoding → Vary: Accept-Encoding always
Security stack: CSP + HSTS + frame-ancestors/XFO + nosniff + Referrer-Policy — ship all, test in Report-Only
Golden rule: any response that varies by a request header MUST declare Vary
Debug recipe 1: curl -v -H 'Accept: ...' -H 'Range: bytes=0-99' --compressed URL; read status + headers
Debug recipe 2: DevTools → Network → Headers/Response tabs; check 'Size' vs 'Time' for compression wins
Debug recipe 3: grep your CDN/proxy config for headers stripped or overridden en route
Common mistakes recap: missing Vary, 206 cached as full body, unsafe-inline CSP, client-trusted X- headers
Trade-off matrix: compression (CPU vs bytes), HSTS preload (security vs lock-in risk), strict CSP (security vs DX)
Ship checklist: correct status codes (406/416/206/304), minimal custom headers, security scan green, docs updated
